newsitem.title: ALBANIA: EU team to Tirana, new pressure for Berisha to go.
newsitem.headline: EU team to Tirana, new pressure for Berisha to go.

text.p: A European Union delegation was due in Tirana on Monday for talks with President Sali Berisha on restoring order after weeks of unrest as Albania's top opposition figure joined calls for him to quit.

Fatos Nano, pardoned by Berisha a week after being released from prison, said he would work with the new all-party government appointed last week after long resistance from the president. But Berisha, he said, had to go.
"I would prefer to shake hands with him as an Albanian citizen and not as president," Nano said of Berisha at his first news conference since his release.

The EU delegation, headed by a Dutch diplomat, was due to hold talks in Rome before travelling on to the Albanian capital, probably by helicopter as the the city's airport remained closed for the fifth day in a row.
The city itself was returning to normal after five days of turmoil. Shops were open, transport was running and public employees obeyed an order from the new all-party government to return to work.

At least 100 people have died in more than a month of unrest sparked by the collapse of popular investment funds, but later mushrooming into a lawless anti-government revolt with country-wide looting of arms from army depots.

European Union foreign ministers approved the mission after a weekend meeting in the Netherlands ruled out Albania's call for military intervention. Ministers pledged to "help Albania restore civilian structures and law and order."

Berisha, who says he will resign if his party loses elections in June, told France's Europe 1 radio station he would ask the EU delegation for police and economic aid to help rebuild Albania's institutions and stabilise the economy.

He said that instead of foreign troops, he would first seek "rather police to start with, because they will work with our police". The situation, he said, remained critical and Albania needed food aid quickly.
"We will request major assistance to rebuild our institutions, also a very quick humanitarian assistance...and economic aid," he said.
Nano, who was briefly prime minister in 1991 and is being mentioned as a possible successor to Berisha, threw his support behind the new government of fellow-socialist Bashkim Fino.
He drew a distinction between demanding that Berisha step aside rather than step down and made clear that he wanted an end to his presidency through the democratic process.

Nano welcomed the prospect of outside aid for Albania, such as the military and police experts promised by the European Union, but said Albania did not need "Blue Helmets" -- a United Nations intervention force.
Jailed in 1993 on corruption charges which he denies as politically inspired, Nano was among 51 prisoners with less than two years to serve who were pardoned by presidential decree.

A state of emergency remains in effect in Albania, with schools closed and a 7 p.m. to 7 a.m. curfew. Helicopters which airlifted hundreds of foreign residents buzzed over the capital for much of the weekend.

Thousands of Albanians fled on rickety boats across the Adriatic to Italy, where Prime Minister Romano Prodi told reporters in the port of Brindisi that Europe would help Albania to rebuild and urged would-be migrants to stay home.
On a beach south of the port of Durres, U.S. marines struck desperate Albanians with rifle butts on Sunday to keep them away from helicopters taking out Americans, Turks and Italians.
